title: Cantar de mio Cid
titleEn: The Song of the Cid — Through Molina to Valencia; the Cid rides Babieca to greet his family (tiradas 84–86, lines 1527–1609)
part: Tiradas 84–86 · Through Molina to Valencia; the Cid rides Babieca to greet his family (lines 1527–1609)
source: Ramón Menéndez Pidal (ed.), Poema de mio Cid, 2.ª edición corregida (Clásicos Castellanos 24; Madrid: Ediciones de “La Lectura”, 1923), pp. 227–232, lines 1527–1609 (tiradas 84–86). Text follows Pidal's critical text exactly, including its old accentuation and mixed spellings; Pidal's italics (his editorial restorations) are shown in [brackets], and a line he restores whole is flagged in its note. Line numbers are Pidal's. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed twelfth-century Castilian. Translations made fresh from the Old Spanish; Pidal's notes and vocabulary (1908–11) the lexical aids.

sentences.t:
Sorrisós de la boca Álbar Fáñez Minaya:
“Ya Ave[n]galvón, amigol sodes sin falla!
sentences.l:
Smiled-himself from the mouth Álbar Fáñez Minaya:
“O Ave[n]galvón, friend-to-him you-are without fail!
sentences.i: Álvar Fáñez Minaya smiled: “Ah, Avengalvón, you are a true friend to him, beyond all doubt!
sentences.n: Tirada 84 (assonance á-a) — the travellers rest at Medinaceli, ride on to Molina, and come near Valencia (Pidal: Los viajeros descansan en Medina. — Parten de Medina a Molina. — Llegan cerca de Valencia). A new assonance, a new tirada: Minaya, falla, alma, nada, adobada, presentaja, stressed á, then a. Minaya answers the Moor's speech that closed tirada 83 (vv. 1520–26). Sorrisós = sonrióse, 'he smiled', the se squeezed to -s; de la boca, 'with his mouth', the stock formula (compare v. 1518). The name runs backwards here, Álbar Fáñez Minaya. Ya, 'O!', the vocative particle (Arabic yā). amigol = amigo le, 'a friend to him', read as 'to the Çid'; the -l could be taken otherwise, so the reading is not certain. sodes = sois, used to one person in respect. sin falla, 'without fail', a common filler of the half-line. The n of Ave[n]galvón is Pidal's (in italics), as again at vv. 1545 and 1551; at v. 1532 the name is printed whole, Avengalvón.

sentences.t:
Si Dios me llegare al Çid e lo vea con el alma,
desto que avedes fecho vos non perderedes nada.
Vayamos posar, ca la çena es adobada.”
sentences.l:
If God me shall-bring to-the Çid and him I-may-see with the soul,
of-this that you-have done you not will-lose nothing.
Let-us-go to-lodge, for the supper is made-ready.”
sentences.i: If God brings me to the Çid, and I see him while there is life in me, you will lose nothing by what you have done. Let us go and take our rest, for the supper is ready.”
sentences.n: llegare, future subjunctive of llegar, here 'to bring (someone) to'; vea, present subjunctive, 'and I may see him'. con el alma, 'with the soul (still in me)', while I live. Pidal's note to v. 1530: 'Luego omite el poeta referir lo que aquí anuncia', the poet does not afterwards tell what is announced here (the requital Minaya promises); he sends to his introduction, p. 85. fecho = hecho (f- for h-). non … nada, the double negative. Vayamos posar, ir + bare infinitive, 'let us go to lodge'. adobada, 'prepared, made ready' (adobar).

sentences.t:
Dixo Avengalvón: “plazme desta presentaja;
antes deste terçer día [a] vos la daré doblada.”
sentences.l:
Said Avengalvón: “it-pleases-me of-this welcome;
before this third day [to] you it I-will-give doubled.”
sentences.i: Avengalvón said: “This welcome pleases me; before three days are out I will repay it to you twice over.”
sentences.n: plazme = me place, 'it pleases me'. Pidal's note to v. 1532: presentaja, 'obsequio, agasajo', 'courtesy, kind treatment'. Here it is most likely Minaya's welcome, the supper and the promise, not a gift of goods as at vv. 516 and 1315 nor an offer of price as at v. 522. la is then the presentaja: he will repay the hospitality doubled, as he does at Molina (vv. 1550–57). antes deste terçer día, 'before this third day', within three days. [a] is Pidal's restoration (in italics); daré, future of dar.

sentences.i: They went into Medinaceli, and Minaya waited on them; all were glad of the service they received, and the king's officer had it paid;
sentences.n: Medina is Medinaceli. sirvíalos = los servía, 'he was serving them': Minaya is host to the Moor's men. Pidal's note to v. 1534: for the day's ride from Molina to Medinaceli that Avengalvón makes here, and makes again on the way back the next day, see v. 2877. tomara[n], 'they had received', the -ra form in its old pluperfect sense; the n is Pidal's (in italics). el portero del rey, the royal officer the king sent with Minaya (v. 1380, where Pidal's note points to these lines). quitar, 'to clear, settle (a debt)': the officer orders the cost met from the king's purse, as Alfonso had promised provisions while they were in his land (v. 1356). The poem treats Medinaceli as the edge of his realm.

sentences.i: so my Çid was honoured, there in Valencia where he was, by as great a feast as they laid out for him in Medinaceli; the king paid for it all, and Minaya goes on his way owing nothing.
sentences.n: ondrado es, 'is honoured': a feast given in the Çid's name honours him though he is far away in Valencia. de, 'by'. conducho, 'provisions, fare' (v. 1488). Medinal = Medina le, 'in Medina … for him', le squeezed onto the place-name; sacara[n], 'they had brought out, laid on', the n Pidal's (in italics). The construction is loose, and the reading of Medinal as Medina le is not certain. quito, 'quit, free of debt', the word of quitar in v. 1536. estava … pagó … va: the epic tense-mixing.

sentences.t:
Passada es la noche, venida es la mañana,
oída es la missa, e luego cavalgavan.
sentences.l:
Passed is the night, come is the morning,
heard is the mass, and at-once they-were-riding.
sentences.i: The night is past, the morning has come, the mass is heard, and straightway they took horse.
sentences.n: Three participles with es, a stock way of passing a night: ser is the auxiliary of verbs of motion (venida es, 'has come') and makes the passive (oída es, 'is heard'). The day begins with mass. luego, 'at once' (not modern 'later'). cavalgavan, imperfect after the presents: tense-mixing again.

sentences.t:
Salieron de Medina, e Salón passavan,
Arbuxuelo arriba privado aguijavan,
el campo de T[a]ranz luégol atravessavan,
vinieron a Molina, la que Ave[n]galvón mandava.
sentences.l:
They-went-out from Medina, and Salón they-were-passing,
Arbuxuelo upward swiftly they-were-spurring,
the field of T[a]ranz at-once-it they-were-crossing,
they-came to Molina, the-one that Ave[n]galvón was-ruling.
sentences.i: They rode out of Medinaceli and crossed the Jalón, spurred swiftly up the Arbujuelo, then crossed the plain of Taranz, and came to Molina, the town that Avengalvón ruled.
sentences.n: The road of vv. 1491–93 travelled in reverse. Salón is the river Jalón below Medinaceli; Arbuxuelo arriba, 'up the Arbujuelo', the stream whose valley the riders came down at v. 1493. privado, 'quickly'; aguijar, 'to spur on'. Pidal's note to v. 1544 sends back to v. 1492: the campo (there Mata) de Taranz is the stony plain above the head of the Arbujuelo valley; the a of T[a]ranz is Pidal's (in italics). luégol = luego le, 'at once … it', le probably taking up el campo; the pronoun is odd and the reading not certain. la que, 'the one which'. mandar, 'to rule, command'.

sentences.i: The bishop Don Jerome, a good Christian beyond all doubt, kept guard over the ladies night and day, with a good warhorse led at his right hand, going on ahead of his arms.
sentences.n: aguarda[va], 'was guarding, attending', the va Pidal's (in italics), as the me of Jero[me] and the e of su[e]s. Pidal's note to v. 1548: cavallo en diestro (Old French cheval en destre, destrier; Latin dexterarius) was the warhorse, a stallion of great size kept for battle; on the road it was led en diestro, at the knight's right, while he rode a palfrey, a horse for travel and display; when need came he got down and found the warhorse at his right, ready to mount by the left stirrup. Behind it went a pack-mule with the arms and baggage, which is what this line expresses: the horse goes ante sues armas, 'before his arms'. The line has no verb of its own; read here as hanging loosely on the one before.

sentences.t: Entre él e Álbar Fáñez hivan a una compaña.
sentences.l: Between him and Álbar Fáñez they-were-going in one company.
sentences.i: He and Álvar Fáñez rode together in one company.
sentences.n: Pidal's note to v. 1549: Entre is pleonastic, used along with the conjunction e, as at v. 191 (Entre Raquel e Vidas): 'he and Álvar Fáñez together'. hivan = ivan, 'they went', the h a spelling only (as in hivalo, v. 1518). a una compaña, 'in one company'.

sentences.i: They have come into Molina, a fine and wealthy town; the Moor Avengalvón served them well, without fail; of all they could wish for they lacked nothing,
sentences.n: Entrados son = han entrado, ser as the auxiliary of a verb of motion. casa, here 'town, city', as Denia la casa (v. 1161) and Valençia la casa (v. 1606). sirvié = servía, the imperfect in -ié. sin falla … non ovieron falla: the same word twice, first in the formula 'without fail', then as the noun 'lack'. de quanto que quisieron, 'of all that they wanted'. ovieron, preterite of aver, 'they had'.

sentences.t:
aun las ferraduras quitar gelas mandava;
a Minaya e a las dueñas ¡Dios cómmo las ondrava!
sentences.l:
even the horseshoes to-settle them-for-them he-was-ordering;
to Minaya and to the ladies, God how them he-was-honoring!
sentences.i: he had even their horseshoes paid for; and Minaya and the ladies — God, how he honoured them!
sentences.n: ferraduras = herraduras, 'horseshoes' (f- for h-). quitar gelas, 'to settle them for them': gelas = ge (le, 'for them') + las (the shoes); quitar as at v. 1536. Pidal's note to v. 1553: 'he ordered even the horseshoes paid for'; paying for the shoeing was a courtesy and sometimes an obligation: a lord, for instance, had to shoe the horse of a vassal he summoned to a meeting (vistas). Dios, cómmo …!, 'God, how …!', the exclamation of wonder. las, feminine plural: either the ladies alone, or Minaya with them, the pronoun agreeing with the nearer noun; the line allows both.

sentences.i: Next morning they rode on at once, and all the way to Valencia he waited on them faithfully; the Moor spent of his own, and took nothing from them.
sentences.n: Otro día manaña, 'the next day, in the morning' (manaña = mañana, so printed). fata = hasta (f- for h-), 'as far as'; fata en Valençia, 'right up to Valencia'. lo so, 'what was his', neuter lo + the possessive so; despendié = gastaba, 'spent'. de[l]los = dellos, de ellos, 'of them', the first l Pidal's (in italics). non … nada, the double negative.

sentences.t:
Con estas alegrías e nuevas tan ondradas
aprés son de Valençia a tres leguas contadas.
sentences.l:
With these joys and news so honored
near are of Valençia at three leagues counted.
sentences.i: With these rejoicings and such honourable tidings they come near to Valencia, three leagues off by count.
sentences.n: alegrías, 'rejoicings'; nuevas, 'news', and also the doings that news is told of; ondradas = honradas. Pidal's note to v. 1559: aprés, 'cerca', 'near'. son, present among the pasts. a tres leguas contadas, 'at three leagues counted', three leagues by reckoning.

sentences.t:
A mio Çid, el que en buen[a] [çinxo espada],
dentro a Valençia el mandád[ol] [leva]van.
sentences.l:
To my Çid, him who in good[-hour] [girded sword],
inside to Valençia the message[-to-him] they-[were-carry]ing.
sentences.i: To my Çid, who in a good hour girded on his sword, they carried the message into Valencia.
sentences.n: The en buen ora formula, shortened: en buen[a] stands for en buena (ora), 'in a good (hour)', as at v. 1603. The a and the words çinxo espada are Pidal's restoration (in italics), made on the model of the formula; so too are ol in mandád[ol] = mandado le, 'the message to him', and leva in [leva]van = llevaban, 'they carried'. dentro a Valençia, 'into Valencia'. Who carries it the poem does not say. Here tirada 84 ends.

sentences.t:
Alegre f[o] mio Çid, que nunqua más nin tanto,
ca de lo que más amava yál viene el mandado.
sentences.l:
Glad wa[s] my Çid, as never more nor so-much,
for of what most he-loved now-to-him comes the message.
sentences.i: My Çid was glad, as never before nor ever so much, for news is coming to him now of those he loved most.
sentences.n: Tirada 85 (assonance á-o) — the Çid sends men out to meet the travellers (Pidal: El Cid envía gentes al encuentro de los viajeros). The line-ends change to tanto, mandado, privado, dalgo, guardando, recabdo: stressed á, then o. It is a tirada of only six lines, and its last line runs straight on into the first of tirada 86. f[o] = fue, the o Pidal's (in italics). que nunqua más nin tanto, 'as never more nor so much': never was he so glad; nunqua = nunca. lo que más amava, neuter, 'what he loved most', his wife and daughters. yál = ya le, 'now … to him'.

sentences.i: He ordered two hundred knights to ride out quickly to receive Minaya and the noble ladies; he himself stayed in Valencia, keeping watch and ward, for he knows well that Álvar Fáñez brings every care with him;
sentences.n: Doz[ien]tos = doscientos, the ien Pidal's (in italics). exir = salir (Latin exire); privado, 'quickly'. reçiban, present subjunctive after the past mandó: tense-mixing. fijas dalgo = hijas de algo, 'daughters of something', of substance and lineage: noble ladies (the word that became hidalgo). sedíe, imperfect of seer, 'sat, stayed'. curiar, 'to watch over' (as curie, v. 1407). He will not leave Valencia unguarded (vv. 1470–72); Pidal's note to v. 1576 recalls this line. recabdo, 'care, precaution', as todo el recabdo at v. 1494. The sentence runs across the tirada break into v. 1568.

sentences.t:
afevos todos aquestos reçiben a Minaya
e a las dueñas e a las niñas e a las otras conpañas.
sentences.l:
behold-you all these receive to Minaya
and to the ladies and to the girls and to the other companies.
sentences.i: and here they are, all of them, receiving Minaya and the ladies and the girls and the rest of the company.
sentences.n: Tirada 86 (assonance á-a) — Don Jerome goes ahead to Valencia to prepare a procession; the Çid rides out to meet Ximena; all enter the city (Pidal: Don Jerónimo se adelanta a Valencia para preparar una procesión. — El Cid cabalga al encuentro de Jimena. — Entran todos en la ciudad). The á-a of tirada 84 comes back: Minaya, conpañas, casa, altas. The tirada begins in mid-sentence, completing v. 1567. afevos, 'behold', the presentative afé + vos (v. 1499), calling on the listeners to look. aquestos = estos, the two hundred knights. dueñas, 'ladies', Ximena and her women; niñas, 'girls', the two daughters; conpañas, 'companies', the rest of the train.

sentences.t:
Mandó mio Çid a los que ha en su[e] casa
que guardassen el alcáç[e]r e las otras torres altas
e todas las puertas e las exidas e las entradas,
sentences.l:
Ordered my Çid to those that he-has in hi[e]s house
that they-should-guard the alcáz[e]r and the other towers high
and all the gates and the exits and the entrances,
sentences.i: My Çid ordered those of his household to guard the citadel and the other high towers, and all the gates, the ways out and the ways in,
sentences.n: a los que ha en su[e] casa, 'those he has in his house', his household men; ha, aver 'to have, hold'. The bracketed e's of su[e] and alcáç[e]r are Pidal's (in italics); alcáçer = alcázar, 'citadel' (Arabic al-qaṣr). guardassen, imperfect subjunctive of guardar. exidas = salidas (exir, 'to go out'). Even in the hour of joy the Çid makes the city safe first (vv. 1566, 1576).

sentences.t:
e aduxiéssenle a Bavieca; poco avié quel ganara
d'aquel rey de Sevilla e de la sue arrancada,
aun non sabié mio Çid, el que en buen ora çinxo espada,
si serié corredor o ssi abrié buena parada;
sentences.i: and that they should bring him Babieca. It was not long since he had won him from that king of Seville, at that king's rout; and my Çid, who in a good hour girded on his sword, did not yet know whether he would prove swift, or whether he would pull up well.
sentences.n: aduxiéssenle, imperfect subjunctive of aduzir, 'to bring', + le, 'to him'; a Bavieca, the personal a before the horse's name. The Çid's horse Babieca is named here for the first time. poco avié quel ganara, 'it was little (time) that he had won him', quel = que le. Verse 1573b is printed wholly in italics in Pidal's edition: it is his restoration, and the label 1573b stands in his own margin; his footnote sends to his introduction (p. 85) for the doubts about this line. It ties the horse to the rout of the king of Seville (vv. 1222–30); la sue arrancada is most naturally that king's defeat. serié corredor, 'would be a runner', fast; buena parada, 'a good stop', the halt from full career. abrié = habría; ssi, the s doubled, a spelling only.

sentences.t:
a la puerta de Valençia, do en so salvo [estava],
delante su mugier e de sus fijas querié tener las armas.
sentences.l:
at the gate of Valençia, where in his safety [he-was],
before his wife and of his daughters he-wanted to-hold the arms.
sentences.i: At the gate of Valencia, where he was safe, before his wife and his daughters, he meant to show his skill at arms.
sentences.n: Pidal's note to v. 1576: do en so salvo [estava], 'where he was in complete safety'; recall the Çid's fears of going far from Valencia (vv. 1566, 1471). [estava] is Pidal's (in italics). Pidal's note to v. 1577: tener las armas = jugar las armas, to exercise in them and show one's skill, at festivities (vv. 1602, 2243), on receiving someone (vv. 2887, 2896) or on seeing someone off (vv. 2613, 2673, 2687). querié = quería. delante su mugier e de sus fijas, with the de given only to the second.

sentences.i: When the ladies had been received with great honour, Bishop Don Jerome went on ahead into the city; he left his horse and made his way to the chapel;
sentences.n: Reçebidas las dueñas, an absolute participle, 'the ladies (being) received'; a una grant ondrança, 'with a great honouring' (ondrança, from ondrar). The bishop goes ahead to make ready a procession (Pidal's rubric). adelant, 'ahead'; se entrava, 'went in', entrar with reflexive se. dexava = dejaba (x = sh). capiella = capilla, 'chapel'. adeliñar, 'to make straight for'.

sentences.t:
con quantos que él puede, que con oras se acordara[n],
sobrepelliças vestidas e con cruzes de plata,
reçibir salién las dueñas e al bueno de Minaya.
sentences.l:
with as-many as he can, who with hours themselves had-made-ready[n],
surplices donned and with crosses of silver,
to-receive they-were-going-out the ladies and the good one of Minaya.
sentences.i: with as many as he can gather, who had made ready in good time, vested in surplices and bearing crosses of silver, they went out to receive the ladies and the good Minaya.
sentences.n: con quantos que él puede, 'with all he can (gather)'. Pidal's note to v. 1581: que con oras se acordaran, 'who had made themselves ready in time' (compare vv. 3058–59), a reading he queries himself; he calls Bello's 'gathered to pray them (the canonical hours)' arbitrary, and cites Hinard's 'who arrived on time'. The phrase is uncertain; it is read here as Pidal reads it. acordara[n], the n Pidal's (in italics). sobrepelliças vestidas, an absolute construction, 'surplices put on': the clergy in procession. reçibir salién, salir + bare infinitive; salién = salían. el bueno de Minaya, 'the good Minaya', the affectionate epic formula.

sentences.t:
El que en buen ora nasco non lo detardava:
vistiós el sobregonel; luenga trahe la barba;
ensiéllanle a Bavieca, cuberturas le echavan,
mio Çid salió sobrél, e armas de fuste tomava.
sentences.l:
He who in good hour was-born not it was-delaying:
put-on-himself the over-tunic; long he-wears the beard;
they-saddle-for-him to Bavieca, trappings on-him they-were-throwing,
my Çid went-out upon-him, and arms of wood he-was-taking.
sentences.i: He who was born in a good hour made no delay: he put on his surcoat — long is the beard he wears; they saddle Babieca for him and throw the trappings over him; my Çid rode out upon him and took up arms of wood.
sentences.n: Pidal prints these lines in the order 1584, 1587, 1585, 1586, moving v. 1587 up and keeping its number; this edition follows his print order and his numbers, as again with vv. 1589 and 1588 below. nasco = nació. detardar, 'to delay'. vistiós = vistióse. Pidal's note to v. 1587: sobregonel is an unknown word; it must be some kind of gonela or silk tunic, probably the garment Fernando II wears in his portrait with armas de fuste (introduction, p. 108); 'surcoat' is a guess. luenga trahe la barba, 'long he wears his beard', the Çid's beard again (v. 1226, el de la luenga barba). ensiéllanle, 'they saddle (for) him'. cuberturas, 'trappings' (v. 1508). sobrél = sobre él. armas de fuste, 'arms of wood': weapons for display and sport, not war.

sentences.t:
Por nombre el cavallo Bavieca cavalga,
fizo una corrida, ésta f[o] tan estraña,
quando ovo corrido, todos se maravillavan;
des día se preçió Bavieca en quant grant f[o] España.
sentences.l:
By name the horse Bavieca he-rides,
he-made a run, this wa[s] so extraordinary,
when he-had run, all themselves were-marvelling;
from-that day himself prized Bavieca in as-much great wa[s] Spain.
sentences.i: The horse he rides is Babieca by name; he made a run, and it was so wondrous; when he had run, all marvelled. From that day Babieca was prized throughout the breadth of Spain.
sentences.n: In Pidal's print order again: v. 1589 stands before v. 1588. Por nombre el cavallo Bavieca, 'the horse Babieca by name'. corrida, 'a run': Pidal's note to v. 1592 calls it a display of horsemanship at the gallop (Old French eslai), a much-used knightly exercise; the Çid runs Babieca again before the king on p. 345 of his edition, in the chronicle prose with which Pidal fills the lost folio after v. 3507 (not given here), and he compares v. 3513, where the Çid recalls that the king bade him run the horse. f[o] = fue, the o Pidal's (in italics). estraña, 'extraordinary'. ovo corrido, 'had run', aver as the perfect auxiliary. des día = desde (aquel) día. se preçió, 'was prized', the reflexive as passive. en quant grant fo España, 'in all that Spain was great', as far as Spain extends.

sentences.i: At the end of the course my Çid dismounted and went straight to his wife and his two daughters; when Doña Ximena saw him, she threw herself at his feet:
sentences.n: Pidal's note to v. 1592: en cabo del cosso, 'at the end of the course' (or of the corrida, v. 1588); he adds that in the Roland Charlemagne and Baligant each run their horse before the whole army ahead of battle (Roland 2997, 3166), and that the eslai was one of the exercises a new knight performed after being dubbed. cosso, 'course, track'. desca[va]lgava, the va Pidal's (in italics), as the e of su[e]s. amas = ambas, 'both'. pie[de]s, the old plural piedes, 'feet', the de Pidal's (in italics): falling at the feet is a gesture of thanks and homage.

sentences.t:
“Merced, Campeador, en buen ora cinxiestes espada!
Sacada me avedes de muchas vergüenças malas;
afeme aquí, señor, yo [e] vuestras fijas amas,
con Dios e convusco buenas son e criadas.”
sentences.l:
“Mercy, Campeador, in good hour you-girded sword!
Drawn me you-have from many shames bad;
behold-me here, lord, I [and] your daughters both,
with God and with-you good they-are and brought-up.”
sentences.i: “Mercy, Campeador! In a good hour you girded on your sword! You have drawn me out of many bitter shames. Here I am, my lord, I and both your daughters: by God's grace and yours they are good and well brought up.”
sentences.n: Merced, 'mercy, thanks', the word of a suppliant. cinxiestes, 2nd pl. preterite of çeñir, 'you girded', the plural of respect; printed with c, not ç. Sacada me avedes, 'you have drawn me out', the participle agreeing with me (Ximena). vergüenças malas, the dishonours of the exile's wife, left behind at San Pedro de Cardeña. afeme, 'behold me', afé + me. [e] is Pidal's restoration (in italics). criadas, 'brought up' (criar). con Dios e convusco, 'with God and with you', thanks to both; convusco = con vos.

sentences.t:
A la madre e a las fijas bien las abraçava,
del gozo que avíen de los sos ojos lloravan.
sentences.l:
To the mother and to the daughters well them he-was-embracing,
from-the joy that they-had from the their eyes they-were-weeping.
sentences.i: He held the mother and the daughters close in his arms; for the joy they had, they wept from their eyes.
sentences.n: A la madre e a las fijas … las: the objects named first and taken up again by the pronoun. abraçava = abrazaba. avíen = habían, aver 'to have'. de los sos ojos lloravan, 'they wept from their eyes', the formula of the poem's first surviving line (v. 1), now for joy; sos = sus, plural 'their'.

sentences.t:
Todas las sus mesnadas en grant deleyt estavan,
armas tenien e tablados [cr]ebanta[van].
sentences.l:
All the his household-troops in great delight were,
arms they-were-holding and board-castles they-were-[br]eak[ing].
sentences.i: All his men were in great delight; they played at arms and broke down the board castles.
sentences.n: mesnadas, 'household troops, retinue'; las sus mesnadas, article + possessive. deleyt = deleite. Pidal's note to v. 1602: 'they played at arms (v. 1577) and broke tablados'; the tablado was a little castle of boards which the knights struck with their lances to bring it down. tenien = tenían. [cr]ebanta[van] = quebrantaban, 'broke', the cr and the van Pidal's (in italics).

sentences.t: Oíd lo que dixo el que en buena [çinxo espada]:
sentences.l: Hear that-which said he who in good [girded sword]:
sentences.i: Hear what he said, he who in a good hour girded on his sword:
sentences.n: Oíd, 'hear!', the minstrel turning to his audience. en buena, 'in a good (hour)', the formula shortened as at v. 1560; çinxo espada is Pidal's restoration (in italics). dixo = dijo (x = sh).

sentences.t:
“vos [doña Ximena], querida mugier e ondrada,
e amas mis fijas mi[o] coraçón e mi alma,
entrad comigo en Valençia la casa,
en esta heredad que vos yo he ganada.”
sentences.l:
“you [lady Ximena], dear wife and honored,
and both my daughters, m[y] heart and my soul,
enter with-me into Valençia the town,
into this inheritance that for-you I have won.”
sentences.i: “You, Doña Ximena, my dear and honoured wife, and both my daughters, my heart and my soul, come with me into the city of Valencia, into this inheritance that I have won for you.”
sentences.n: [doña Ximena] and the o of mi[o] are Pidal's restorations (in italics); mio coraçón, 'my heart', beside mi alma, 'my soul'. comigo = conmigo. Valençia la casa, 'Valencia the city' (as at v. 1550). heredad, 'heritage, land held by right', the word the Çid used of Valencia at v. 1472. vos yo he ganada, 'I have won for you', the participle agreeing with heredad; he, aver as perfect auxiliary.

sentences.t:
Madre e fijas las manos le besavan.
A tan grand ondra ellas a Valençia entravan.
sentences.l:
Mother and daughters the hands to-him were-kissing.
With so great honor they into Valençia were-entering.
sentences.i: Mother and daughters kissed his hands. With such great honour they entered Valencia.
sentences.n: besar las manos, the kiss of the hands, homage and thanks; le, 'his', the dative of the person. A tan grand ondra, 'with such great honour'. Here tirada 86 ends; tirada 87 takes the ladies up into the alcázar to look out over Valencia.
